hook.text: In 1943, the statistician Abraham Wald took on a wartime question. Which parts of a bomber are the most vulnerable?

evidence.text: The evidence was the damage on the planes that made it home.

instinct.text: And the military's instinct was to protect the parts with the most holes.

example.text: Wald's memos work through an example. Four hundred planes fly a mission... and three hundred fifty-nine come back.

engines.text: The two engines are more than a quarter of the plane. But they carry fewer than one in five of the holes.

fuselage.text: The fuselage carries more than its share.

missing.text: So where are the missing engine hits? On the planes that never came back.

estimate.text: In his numbers, one hit to an engine downs a plane thirty-nine times in a hundred. One to the fuselage... about five.

holes.text: The holes show where a plane can be hit and still come home. The protection belongs where they AREN'T.

funds.text: Business data plays the same trick. Take five thousand simulated mutual funds, averaging six percent a year.

close.text: Now close every fund that lost more than four percent, and drop it from the database.

gone.text: That's five hundred and fifteen funds... gone.

left.text: Average the funds that are left, and you get seven point six five.

deleted.text: Not one fund got better. The losers were just deleted.

habit.text: The planes that made it home. The funds still open. The customers who stayed.

ask.text: When your data is whoever's still here... ask what's missing from it, and why.

next.text: Even a fair sample, drawn from everyone, won't hit the truth exactly.

far.text: So how far off can it be?
